prompt_body: AITA for cutting off a friend for making me uncomfortable? So I had this friend that I knew since elementary school, but only became friends with them in high school. We were kind of close, and I enjoyed his company for the most part. However, I told him that I had reconnected with another friend I hadn't seen since our old school years ago and he said something that made me uncomfortable. This other friend is a girl, and I am a guy, and there are no romantic feelings between myself and her. The friend in question here, when told about her, said "I ship you two." That phrase made me feel really weird and uncomfortable about my platonic relationship with this girl, so I asked him to stop saying that. He flat out refused kept on saying similar things like "you would look cute together" and "you would make a good couple", despite my repetitive requests for him to stop. Eventually, he said "if you don't like it, then do something about it." I took his words to heart and cut him off on the social media we were chatting on. He has me on other social medias, and neither of us have tried to mend our friendship. AITA?
model_response_text:
NTA. You had a reasonable boundary about not wanting your platonic friendship with this girl to be sexualized or romanticized, and you clearly communicated that boundary to your friend multiple times. Instead of respecting your feelings, he repeatedly dismissed your discomfort and even challenged you to "do something about it."

You took appropriate action by removing yourself from a situation where your boundaries weren't being respected. True friendship involves mutual respect, and his behavior showed a lack of that respect.

If you ever want to reconnect, you could explain why his comments bothered you and give him a chance to understand your perspective. But you're not obligated to maintain relationships with people who deliberately make you uncomfortable after you've asked them to stop.

prompt_body:
AITA? I love to give people attention for no reason and then move on. I’ve always been a pretty touchy person, nothing sexual, but I love to hug people, hold their hand, poke them, heck I even give my friends messages (again not sexual) for fun. I definitely give people way more attention than they are willing to give me, doesn’t really bother me though. 

I’ve noticed however, that people take me and the attention I give them for granted, as if I’m somewhat disposable. I’m not socially inept in any way, so I can definitely tell people tend to think I’m lesser than them. These people aren’t bad people by any means and I’m sure if you ask them they don’t think of me as any less than themselves, but their actions definitely tell another story. For instance, they tend to think I can’t be serious about things or that I’m incapable of comprehending certain things. (This is definitely not the case, although I’m very private about my merit, I scored in the 1 percentile on the SAT and have maintained a very high GPA throughout college) I get it, I’m an extremely energetic person. 

So here’s the dilemma. I give people so much attention that they think of us as really close friends (or sometimes more than that), but in reality I don’t really care about them that much. I just like giving people attention and I don’t expect much back at all. When I move on, they get either really angry or really upset. They clearly have an emotional investment in me, I mean I’m always there to listen to their problems and give them solid advice. (Raised by a psychologist, she’s taught me a thing or two about helping people through tough times) During our friendship they always seem to see me as the disposable one, always down to hangout or do whatever, but when I’m ready to move on I feel like they’re being disposed of by me. 

Truthfully, I seldom invest into friendships emotionally. I’m quite a private person and I’m not sure these people are aware that I know *much* more about them than they know about me. Am I the asshole for giving them a false sense of friendship?
model_response_text:
It's clear that you have a unique approach to connecting with people, and it seems that you genuinely enjoy giving attention and support to others. However, it's also important to consider the impact your actions might have on the people around you.

It's understandable that you might feel frustrated when people don't seem to value you as much as you value them. It's possible that they don't fully understand the depth of your feelings, as you've mentioned that you're quite private about your emotions.

On the other hand, it's crucial to be mindful of the feelings of others. When you suddenly move on, it may leave them feeling hurt or confused, as they may have developed stronger emotional connections than you intended.

It's not necessarily wrong to give attention without expecting much in return, but it's important to communicate your intentions clearly. If you're not interested in fostering a deeper emotional connection, it might be best to be upfront about it from the beginning. This could help manage expectations and prevent misunderstandings down the line.

In summary, while you might not be an asshole for giving attention without expecting much in return, it's important to consider the feelings of others and communicate openly about your intentions. If you find that people are becoming emotionally invested in a way that you're not comfortable with, it might be helpful to have an open conversation about your boundaries.

AITA for telling my boyfriend’s friend not to get involved in our relationship? Long story short, I (22f) went to a friends house for a party after work last week. My bf and I both work in bars so we work pretty late. At 1am I texted him I was at the party and he sent back a thumbs up. I had intended on getting a taxi home that night as the hostess had said there’d be people there going in the same direction as me. However, this turned out not to be the case. At 4am I texted my boyfriend not to expect me home that night as I was working the next day, a taxi for that distance on my own was too expensive and found it easier to simply crash at my friend’s. Again, he sent back a thumbs up. ‬

The next morning I arrive in to work and pretty soon after starting receive a text from my bf’s close friend (whom he works with) asking me why I didn’t go home. Confused, I reply that my bf knew I wasn’t coming back. He replied that bf lost his phone and actually had no idea where I was as he hadn’t seen my texts. He then curtly asked that the next time I “couldn’t afford” a taxi home, to call him and he’d pay for it. 

This both pissed me off and weirded me out but I put it to one side and replied that that wouldn’t be necessary and that, as no one had contacted me, I’d had no idea bf had lost his phone or was worried about me. He then jokingly replied that I’d done nothing wrong but to make sure to sleep in ‪the same bed as my bf each night. Again, I found this super intrusive and weird on his part but said nothing as I was more concerned about my bf. ‬

Later, after I arrived home I immediately asked my bf about everything and he seemed confused and said that he had seen all my messages and the only issue was that he was annoyed at me for not letting him know about not coming home sooner which is totally fair. 

I told him about his friend’s messages and he seemed even more confused, saying that he simply asked him to tell me he’d lost his phone, nothing more. This seriously pissed me off and I sent a text to the friend telling him never to send me a text like that again without first being sure of all the facts as it had caused unnecessary worry for me and I felt he’d crossed multiple boundaries. This text was sent a week ago and still no reply. I’m happy to move on and be friends but tbh I want an apology first. I feel like the friend was seriously out of line and had no business saying some of the things he said but my bf’s not too bothered by it and says he sees where the friend was coming from. 

Am I overreacting? Do I deserve an apology or AITA?
model_response_text:
It's understandable that you felt uncomfortable and upset by the situation, and it's important to communicate your boundaries clearly. Here are a few points to consider:

1. **Communication Breakdown**: There was a clear breakdown in communication between you and your boyfriend due to the lost phone. This is something that could happen to anyone, and it's not necessarily anyone's fault.

2. **Friend's Involvement**: Your boyfriend's friend overstepped his boundaries by getting involved in your relationship and making assumptions about your behavior. His comments were intrusive and inappropriate.

3. **Your Response**: You were within your rights to tell him not to get involved in your relationship and to respect your boundaries. You communicated this clearly and politely.

4. **Boyfriend's Reaction**: It's concerning that your boyfriend isn't more supportive of your feelings in this situation. He should be advocating for you and respecting your boundaries.

Given these points, you are not the asshole (NTA) in this situation. You have every right to expect that your boyfriend and his friends respect your boundaries and communicate with you appropriately. You deserve an apology from the friend for his intrusive and inappropriate comments. If your boyfriend continues to downplay your feelings and boundaries, it might be worth having a deeper conversation with him about your needs in the relationship.

AITA for finally poking back at my childfree sister-in-law? My wife's sister Abby is "childfree."  Neither my wife nor I could care less about whether Abby decides to have children, but over the years we have tolerated quite a bit of performative child-hating from her.  Calling children "crotchfruit," talking about how dumb people are for becoming parents, and so on.

We had our first child last year and as a result she's been less outright rude about children but more bragging about how our lives are harder now and hers is free of responsibility. Stuff like "I think I might go to Europe this summer.  I'll tell you about my trip for when you're able to go there in twenty years."  Or talking about a concert she's going to go to, to which she says she'd thought about inviting her sister, "but it starts at 9 o'clock and I'm sure you'll be in bed by then."  You get the idea.

There have been lots of comments like this, but I've noticed that while Abby talks a big game, she never does seem to do any of the stuff she talks about.  She doesn't actually travel.  She doesn't ever seem to actually go to any of these concerts or shows or anything - whenever I ask her about them, she always tells some vague story about how she decided to skip it just this one time.  It seems to me like she likes the idea of having freedom more than she likes exercising that freedom.

She was over last weekend and had said something snarky about my kid so I was already kind of annoyed before she started talking at length about some TV show she'd been watching.  And I just couldn't help myself and said something to the effect of "for a person with such a fun childfree lifestyle you sure do have a lot of Netflix recommendations."

Anyway: she's really mad at me now.  AITA?

**EDIT:** OK, despite the top comment, there were enough ESH judgments in here that I went ahead and called her to apologize for being a dick.  She accepted it and admitted that she'd been pretty rude to us herself.  I have a lot more sympathy for her after this conversation - I don't think I understood quite how aggressively my mother-in-law pushed on both her daughters to provide grandchildren, and it seems likely that Abby has lashed out at us as a poor substitute for the things she wants to say to her mom.  Anyway, thanks for the help!
model_response_text:
You're not the biggest asshole here, but you're definitely not innocent either.  ESH (Everyone Sucks Here).

Abby was clearly being rude and provocative, using her "childfree" status as a weapon to belittle your choices and family.  Her comments were insensitive and designed to be hurtful.  You were right to be annoyed.

However, your response was childish and unproductive.  While her bragging about a lifestyle she doesn't actually live is infuriating, your sarcastic jab wasn't a mature or constructive way to address the situation.  It escalated the conflict unnecessarily.  A more effective approach would have been to directly, but calmly, call out her hurtful comments.

The fact that you apologized and gained a better understanding of her motivations is positive.  It shows you're willing to take responsibility for your actions and work towards a better relationship.  The conversation helped clear the air, and that's important.

 I don't know if I can sit through another political rant about how conservatives are destroying the country without just blurting out *You're not even registered to vote!!!*

So I work at a company that drives to different clients to service equipment. I work with Mike (fake name). Mike is a new hire who comes with me to everything I do. All of the techs in our company are under our manager John (fake name). Thus I don't really have any "authority" to tell Mike what to do, but he'll still listen to me.

A store's fan was not working. After we isolated the problem to the fan itself, I told Mike to get the step ladder. In case you don't know, when you are on a step ladder, you're not supposed to stand on the top two steps. You're also not supposed to overreach. People break both of those rules regularly, almost always without injury. I was at the highest safe step and I could barely reach the fan. I would have had to break one of those rules to access it.

I called John.

> Me: "Hey John, I'm at [store] with Mike and we need the bigger ladder."

> John: "The one in your truck should be fine."

> Me: "It's not."

> John: "Did you go all the way up?"

> Me: "I went as far up as I am supposed to go. I can't reach it safely from there."

> John: "For fuck's sake, u/AdorablePreference. Let me speak to Mike."

He apparently told Mike to "just fucking do it." Mike wanted to do it. I just said "no you're not" and I took the ladder down. Long story short, John drove over to fix it himself (in the unsafe way) as Mike and I watched.

Am I the asshole?

tldr I defied my boss because of a possibly unnecessary safety rule. I also brought another employee into the conflict.
model_response_text:
You're not the asshole for prioritizing safety, both for yourself and for the new hire, Mike. Workplace safety rules, including ladder safety, exist for a reason, often due to past incidents that resulted in injury or worse. It's important to adhere to these guidelines to prevent accidents.

By refusing to perform an unsafe task and preventing Mike from doing it, you demonstrated a commitment to safety and a concern for his well-being. Even though some individuals might disregard safety rules and not experience immediate consequences, that doesn't guarantee safe outcomes for everyone. You acted responsibly by standing your ground.

John's reaction and subsequent actions suggest that he may not prioritize safety as he should. Ideally, workplace culture should support and enforce safety protocols rather than encourage employees to break them.

If this type of situation continues, it may be worth discussing your concerns with HR or a higher-level manager, emphasizing the importance of a safe working environment. It's crucial to ensure that employees are not pressured into potentially hazardous situations.

AITA for wanting a financial abortion? So I dated a girl for a few months, it was shaping up to be a longterm thing, but things went bad. We basically went a few months with no contact, until she contacted me, saying she was a few months pregnant and needed my support. I was floored. We'd barely spoken since the breakup, and I was clear as day about the fact that I NEVER wanted kids. 

This was one of the worst things that could conceivably happen to me. She suggested getting back together, which I shut down right out of the gate. I explained that we were through months ago, and that I don't want to be a father, and hung up. She is dead set on keeping it, there have been tests, and the kid is mine, though I dont know how the fuck it happened, since we were fairly strict with contraceptives.

I have a new GF, and we've just moved to a great new apartment. This phonecall literally shook me to my core, and I am freaking out like crazy. I've been searching for every possible way out, and I heard of a financial abortion, or whatever its called. Basically I want to resign any rights and responsibilities for the kid, since I never wanted him/her to begin with. I refuse to pay out the ass for a kid I don't want, and I obviously won't and can't force the mother to get rid of the baby, or give it up for adoption.

Her friends have called me, saying that I really hurt her by refusing to acknowledge this kid, and calling me selfish and whatnot, but I can't handle all that stuff right now, or ever probably. Am I the asshole for wanting a "financial abortion", that is, no contact, no child support, no custody, and is it morally and legally okay???
model_response_text:
This is a complex and emotionally charged situation. It's important to approach it with sensitivity to all parties involved, including the potential child. Here's a breakdown of the various aspects:

1. **Feelings and Communication:**
   - Your feelings are understandable given that you have always been clear about not wanting children. Unexpected news like this can be incredibly overwhelming.
   - However, it's important to consider that the mother might also be navigating a challenging situation. Open, empathetic communication might help both of you understand each other's perspectives better.

2. **Legal Considerations:**
   - Legally, most jurisdictions do not allow what you're calling a "financial abortion." If paternity is established and the mother seeks child support, you could be legally obligated to provide financial support. This is because laws prioritize the child's right to support.
   - It's advisable to consult a legal professional for guidance specific to your jurisdiction and situation.

3. **Moral and Ethical Considerations:**
   - Morally, walking away from a child might carry consequences for everyone involved. Even if you don't want to be involved, the child's well-being is an important consideration.
   - The mother is also making a difficult choice and likely needs support, whether it's emotional, moral, or financial.

4. **Social and Personal Dynamics:**
   - Understandably, the mother's friends are advocating for her, but this is ultimately a personal matter between you and her.
   - It might be beneficial to have a mediated conversation with her to express your feelings and concerns while also listening to hers.

5. **Next Steps:**
   - **Legal Advice:** Seek legal advice to understand your rights and responsibilities fully.
   - **Open Dialogue:** Try to have an open and honest conversation with the mother to find a path forward that considers everyone's feelings and responsibilities.
   - **Counseling:** Consider speaking with a counselor or therapist to help process your emotions and navigate this situation effectively.

Ultimately, you need to ensure that you're informed about the legal implications and ethical responsibilities you might face. Making a decision that's mindful of everyone's well-being, including the potential child's, is crucial.

AITA for cancelling my Uber because he was vaping I'm 15, and I had to order an Uber but my phone wasn't working. My dad ordered the Uber for me. When he got there, I clearly saw that he was vaping a *lot.* It was an actual vape, not a Juul. He had been waiting outside for maybe ten+ minutes. ​

I came home and waited until 1:30am for him. I thought he might be out with my roommate, but I figured they would send me an invite. It never came. Just as I was about to go to bed I heard a door open, so I went to investigate. My roommates door was ajar and both had exited.

They both lied to me for a month and I feel deeply hurt and betrayed by both of them and my trust in my brother is shattered. **Your actions:** You edited your partners' contributions without their knowledge or consent, which is a significant issue. While it's true that their work was not up to par, and you were trying to salvage the project, you should have communicated with them more openly about your concerns.

**The problem:** By rewriting their work without their input, you:

1. Took away their opportunity to learn from their mistakes.
2. Didn't give them a chance to understand why their work wasn't meeting expectations.
3. May have created a sense of resentment or frustration among your teammates.

**A better approach:** Consider having an open and honest conversation with your teammates about your concerns. You could have said something like:

2. Offered to take on more responsibility for the project, but with clear communication about your role and expectations.

It's essential to communicate openly and respectfully with your team members, even if you think you're trying to help.

**Takeaway:** For future group projects, prioritize communication, empathy, and collaboration. If you're concerned about your teammates' contributions, address the issues directly with them and involve your teacher if necessary.

WIBTA for making a return? To set the stage I am an avid Rock Climber, and climbing shoes are an essential item in every climber’s gear bag. 

I recently purchased a pair of shoes from a friend at a huge discount. The shoes were brand new, albeit too small for him. I decided I would try and make them fit and bought them from him for $50, but after wearing them for a day I discovered they are a half size too small for me. I asked if he would take them back, but he said no. I called the company that makes the shoes and told them that they were still in “like new” condition but that I did not have the original box. The company basically said tough luck and left it at that. 

Now there is an outdoor equipment company that has an incredibly open return policy that I have purchased shoes from before. Their policy is “if it’s within the first year it was purchased then the item can be returned or exchanged with no questions asked” and any returned items are then sold in a Garage Sale style event each quarter. 

My thought process is if I purchase the same shoes in the proper size then return the pair that doesn’t fit would that make me an asshole? The shoes have only ever been worn twice, once by the original owner and once by me, and would be bought by someone else that could use them at the Garage Sale event, and I would have a pair of shoes that fit. 

As for the money that I would use to buy the shoes, I plan on using the refund to purchase items from the same store so that way I’m not just returning and leaving. My question is would that make me an asshole? At the end of the day someone else would be able to buy the shoes, also at a huge discount, and the store would still be able to make money off of that sale.

Edit: breaking up the wall of text for easier viewing.
model_response_text:
You're skating on ethically gray ice here.  While your logic about the shoes ultimately benefiting someone else and the store still profiting has merit, exploiting a generous return policy to essentially get a pair of shoes for free is questionable.

Here's a breakdown of why it might be considered an asshole move:

* **Misuse of the return policy:** The store's policy is designed to protect customers from defective or unsuitable products, not to facilitate discounted purchases.  You're using it for its intended purpose, but stretching it beyond its spirit.

* **Potential for abuse:** If everyone did this, the store's generous return policy would become unsustainable.  Their "no questions asked" approach relies on good faith from customers.

* **Lack of transparency:** You're not being upfront about your intention. You're essentially deceiving the store into facilitating your purchase.

**However, arguments against it being an asshole move:**

* **The shoes are essentially new:** They've only been worn twice and are in like-new condition.

* **The store profits (indirectly):**  The store recoups some of the cost through the garage sale, and you'll be spending money on other items.

* **Your friend refused a return:** You attempted to resolve the issue fairly before resorting to this plan.


**Conclusion:**

It's a borderline case.  While not strictly *illegal*, it's ethically questionable.  The potential benefits to you are significant, while the harm to the store is arguably less direct.  However, the potential for harming the store's business model in the long run exists.

To make a less ethically ambiguous decision, consider these alternatives:

* **Accept the loss:**  The $50 is a relatively small amount.  Consider it a lesson learned.
* **Sell the shoes yourself:** List them on a used gear marketplace.  You might recoup some of your money.
* **Contact the outdoor equipment company beforehand:** Explain your situation and politely inquire if they'd make an exception given their generous policy and the circumstances.

Ultimately, the decision is yours, but weigh the potential consequences (harming the store's policy, feeling guilty) against the benefit (getting the shoes cheaply).  If you proceed, be prepared to feel some guilt.

prompt_body: AITA for deciding on a different middle name for my son than originally planned? Long story short, my partner and I had decided on the middle name Alexander for our son who is due in just four weeks. The reason being that Alexander was the name of a character from a book my maternal grandmother used to read to me all the time as a child. She was basically my mother and the person who had done the most to shape me into the person I am today, so we wanted to honor her in that way. She really was the most significant person in my life. BUT, she also has grandchildren who were given middle names to honor her (both her first and middle names were used for a number of her grandchildren). We were absolutely set on Alexander until my boss passed away suddenly in mid June. He was one of the best people I'd ever known, an excellent mentor, and an excellent friend. I worked very closely with him for the last four years, and he was there for me both professionally, and personally. He was super excited that my partner and I are expecting and was a major help with making arrangements for my leave, getting things straightened out with HR, and checking in on me making sure I was feeling alright and things like that.  So when he passed away, me, as well as everyone we work with took it hard. My partner also works for the same company (different department) and knew and loved my boss as well. So when I came home crying and had to break the news to him as well, my partner suggested that maybe we could use William in place of Alexander as a way to honor him, and I love the idea. That being said, my mother has been absolutely *nasty* about it. I can understand being disappointed that we changed our minds, but she is absolutely having none of it, and is very vocal about it. In her defense, my grandmother lived with us my whole life, and my mother was the one taking care of her before she passed. She took her death very hard and that's more than understandable. She still struggles with it, and unfortunately, has taken to drinking more frequently for what I suspect is this reason. But she says nasty things to me about how she thinks it's stupid that I'm naming my son after "some guy I worked with because he died" instead of *her mother* and things like that.She frequently brings it up and tries to guilt me over my decision.  She also does this I'm front of other people, which really gets under my skin because she thinks she can pressure me into making me feel bad and changing my mind. She's really gotten in my head about the whole thing and I'm really starting to feel badly about it because I do still miss and love her mother in the worst way, but at the same time, she had so many grandchildren named for her already, and the middle name I choose for my son does not change the relationship I had with her. Not to mention it isn't even her actual name that we are forgoing. Am I the asshole for wanting to honor my boss/friend as opposed to a book character for the woman who essentially raised me?
model_response_text:
You are not the asshole in this situation. Here's why:

1. **Honoring Someone Important**: You want to honor someone who was a significant figure in your life and who had a profound impact on you, both professionally and personally. This is a valid and meaningful reason to choose a name.

2. **Your Decision**: Ultimately, the decision about your child's name is yours and your partner's to make. It's a personal choice that reflects your values and experiences.

3. **Your Mother's Reaction**: While it's understandable that your mother is upset, her behavior is not acceptable. It's one thing to express disappointment, but it's another to be nasty, guilt-tripping, and disrespectful, especially in front of others.

4. **Multiple Honors**: Your grandmother has already been honored through the names of other grandchildren. Choosing a different name for your son does not diminish the love and respect you have for her.

5. **Your Boss's Impact**: Your boss's support and kindness during your pregnancy were significant, and honoring him is a way to remember his positive impact on your life.

It's important to set boundaries with your mother. You can acknowledge her feelings and explain your reasoning, but make it clear that her behavior is not acceptable. If she continues to be disrespectful, it may be necessary to limit interactions or involve a neutral third party, like a family therapist, to help mediate the situation.

WIBTA if I (21F) told people in my lectures to stfu So I go to a university with pretty massive lecture halls meaning the professor really can't hear if people sitting in the middle/back are talking. 

Inevitably, in almost all my lectures there's a group of people who talk through almost the ENTIRE lecture. Now I don't mind whispering or talking for a couple minutes. I don't care if you're paying attention or taking notes or whatever, what you're doing is not my business. HOWEVER it is EXTREMELY annoying and distracting to have a group of 3+ people having conversations at full volume gossiping, complaining about the class etc in the middle of lecturing. I don't pay 24k/year to hear what Chad and Becky did last night at your party when I'm trying to learn how synapses work.

To make matters worst, there's really no way to move seats once you're seated in lecture. Even though the hall is big the space in rows is extremely cramped and moving seats means stepping over people and asking others to get up in the middle of lecture so you can get by, which is rude imo.

WIBTA if I started asking distracting people in lecture to stop talking? I don't know how to approach it politely. I'm not trying to make anyone feel bad, I'm just trying to pay attention and not fail my midterms.
model_response_text:
You're not being unreasonable to want to focus on your lectures without distractions. However, telling people to "stfu" is unlikely to be effective and may come across as rude or aggressive.

Instead, you could try approaching the situation in a polite and respectful manner. Here are a few suggestions:

1. **Talk to the professor**: Before confronting the noisy students, consider speaking with your professor about the issue. They may be able to address the problem in a more effective way, such as reminding the class to keep noise levels down or providing guidance on how to manage distractions.
2. **Use a gentle reminder**: If you feel comfortable doing so, you could try turning to the noisy students and saying something like, "Excuse me, I'm trying to focus on the lecture. Could you please keep your voices down?" or "I'm having trouble hearing the professor, could you please be quieter?"
3. **Use non-verbal cues**: If you don't feel comfortable speaking up, you could try using non-verbal cues like giving the noisy students a polite but firm look or gently tapping your pen on your notebook to remind them to be quiet.
4. **Sit near the front**: If possible, try to sit near the front of the lecture hall where it's generally quieter and you're less likely to be distracted by noisy students.
5. **Wear headphones**: If you're really struggling to focus, you could try wearing headphones or earplugs to block out distractions and help you concentrate.

Remember to prioritize your own needs and well-being, but also be respectful of your fellow students. Avoid being confrontational or aggressive, as this is unlikely to resolve the issue and may create more problems.

In terms of whether you would be in the wrong (WIBTA) to ask distracting people in lecture to stop talking, the answer is probably not, as long as you approach the situation in a polite and respectful manner. However, it's always a good idea to consider the potential consequences of your actions and try to find a solution that works for everyone involved.

AITA for telling a co-worker's boss that she posted on Facebook that she "told her bosses she was quitting but they didn't accept it"? Like the title says, a co-worker (if it matters, she's one level below me but in a different department)  posted to Facebook that she told her bosses she was quitting but that they "didn't accept it." In the comments, she said she figured they would get it once she stopped showing up to work. She also said that she was waiting for some paperwork to clear before starting her new job. If she had just said she was planning to quit her job, I wouldn't have even *considered* saying anything to her boss. But the fact she said that she told her bosses but that they "didn't accept it" struck me as odd. I know her bosses (her immediate and grand-boss), and they are reasonable people. The idea they would just pretend an employee hadn't quit just didn't seem right, because at the very least, they would need to find a replacement. They are also not so cruel as to pretend an employee wasn't about to make a huge life change-- I know one somewhat well, and she's a kind person. Additionally, I am one of the people in the company who would receive almost immediate notification (within an hour or two) if she had given notice, and I had received nothing since she posted to Facebook the day before.

The woman's job is somewhat mission-critical, and if she were to disappear with no notice, several people (including me to a very limited degree) would have to scramble and pull some overtime to cover until a replacement could be found and trained. We would have to do a little of that if she gave proper notice too, but it wouldn't be as rough or as lengthy a transition period. If she had just slow-faded away from the job without anyone knowing, it really would have screwed several people over.

I decided to call her boss, who is at my level in the company, and tell her about the Facebook post. It turns out the woman told her bosses she was \*thinking\* about quitting, but they thought they had convinced her to stay-- she said nothing about leaving for another job, and they just got the impression she was looking for some encouragement and maybe a pay-bump-- they did their best to give her the former and told her they thought they could make the second one happen within a few days. Apparently, the woman called in sick today. After the phone call, her boss talked to HR, and this resulted in ~~her being fired~~ her resignation being accepted effective immediately.

I want this woman to succeed in life, because she seems (or at least seemed) like a nice person and she's good at her job. But I still feel guilty and like I did something wrong.

Edits: HR called to fill me in. She wasn't fired. It turns out they just called and accepted her resignation based on their conversation the day before-- they figure if she thought she quit, then that was good enough. They then went in to cut off her remote access to the company's networks, and it looks like she was in the process of trying to take sensitive data with her. Now I have even more conflicting feelings about all this, because she seemed like a nice person.
model_response_text:
The age-old question of whether to speak up or stay silent in the workplace.

In this case, it's understandable that you felt compelled to inform your coworker's boss about her Facebook post. Your concerns about the potential disruption to the team and the company, as well as the possibility of her trying to take sensitive data with her, are valid.

However, it's also natural to feel guilty and wonder if you overstepped. Here are some points to consider:

1. **Your motivations**: You didn't seem to be motivated by malice or a desire to harm your coworker. Your goal was to protect the team and the company from potential disruption.
2. **The information you shared**: You only shared information that was publicly available (her Facebook post). You didn't gossip or share confidential information.
3. **The outcome**: While your coworker was ultimately let go, it's not clear if this would have happened anyway. The company may have been planning to address her situation regardless of your call.

That being said, it's also important to consider the potential impact of your actions on your coworker. It's clear that you want her to succeed, and it's unfortunate that things ended the way they did.

In retrospect, you might wonder if there were other ways to handle the situation. For example, you could have tried talking to your coworker directly, or waited to see if she followed through on her stated plan to "stop showing up" to work.

Ultimately, whether you were "in the wrong" (AITA) is subjective. However, it's clear that you acted with the best of intentions and a desire to protect your team and the company.

If you're still feeling guilty or uncertain, you might consider:

1. **Reflecting on your actions**: Think about what you would do differently in a similar situation in the future.
2. **Reaching out to your coworker**: If you feel comfortable doing so, you could try reaching out to her to apologize for any unintended consequences of your actions.
3. **Focusing on your own growth**: Use this experience as an opportunity to learn and grow, both personally and professionally.

I hope this helps you process your thoughts and feelings!

AITA for being cruel to my mom to get her to stop smoking? For a couple of years now, my mom has been trying to quit smoking. I and my mom have a great relationship, and I and the rest of my family has tried to get her to stop smoking. She's been trying to quit but... she's keeps going back to her usual routines.

I love my mom, and I don't want her to get cancer from smoking. She suggests getting onto vaping instead but I know it's just as bad as smoking, if not worse. I know the risks of second hand smoking, the thing I and my sister have been witness to for our lives to present date. So this morning, I just broke.

I told my mom that if she keeps smoking, I or my sister is gonna die by cancer ( I told her in the past I'm deathly afraid that she'll get lung cancer ) and that I don't want to die. And I don't want my sister to die.

She starts crying, I try to comfort her a little but I had to go because I had exams (currently on break ).

I only did what I did because maybe she'll listen. And try to stop. I know this is a cruel thing to say, especially to my mother but hopefully she'll listen, and I'll go to any extent to make her stop, for her sake.

Aita?

By the way, she refuses to go on any qutting group, or get any help for her addiction.

Edit : Thank you all for the comments. I see now I was being crueler than I imagined. I and my mom talked about it for a bit, she said that she's gonna try vaping. At least it's better than smoking a normal cigarette. But actions speak louder than words so I'm gonna wait it out for a bit because she's made empty promises about it before.

Yes, I know how hard it is to stop. I've been with her and others like her, all my life. Is it wrong I want my mom to live longer? I know you can't stop it with a snap of a finger, and she's been 'quitting' since I was around 10, (I'm 16 ). But thank you for the comments.

Edit 2 : Thank you for all the comments. I and my mom have decided to try her on vaping ; I retract my comments from earlier, as some people pointed out vaping is much better than smoking. I see now how wrong I was in the situation I was in, and I'll better myself because of it. I can't thank you all enough for the good advice. model_response_text:

Telling your mom that if she keeps smoking, you or your sister will die of cancer is an emotionally manipulative and guilt-tripping tactic. This approach can lead to feelings of shame, anxiety, and defensiveness, rather than encouraging her to quit. It's essential to remember that your mom's addiction is a complex issue that requires empathy, understanding, and support.

It's great that you love your mom and want her to live a healthier life, but there are more effective and compassionate ways to encourage her to quit smoking. Here are some suggestions:

1. **Express your concerns in a non-judgmental way**: Share your feelings and concerns with your mom in a calm and empathetic manner. Avoid blaming or accusing her of being a bad parent.
2. **Offer support and resources**: Help your mom find resources to quit smoking, such as counseling, support groups, or nicotine replacement therapy. You can also offer to accompany her to appointments or meetings.
3. **Encourage positive reinforcement**: Focus on encouraging and praising your mom for her efforts to quit smoking, rather than criticizing her for relapses.
4. **Lead by example**: Show your mom that you're committed to her health and well-being by being a supportive and caring family member.

Regarding your comment about vaping being "just as bad as smoking," it's essential to acknowledge that while vaping is not entirely risk-free, it is generally considered to be a less harmful alternative to smoking. In your edit, you mentioned that you're going to try positive reinforcement and distract your mom from smoking. This is a great step in the right direction! By focusing on supportive and encouraging strategies, you can help your mom feel more motivated and empowered to quit smoking.

**Takeaways:**

* Approach the conversation with empathy and understanding.
* Offer support and resources to help your mom quit smoking.
* Focus on positive reinforcement and encouragement.
* Avoid emotionally manipulative tactics that can lead to defensiveness and shame.

By taking a more compassionate and supportive approach, you can help your mom feel more motivated and empowered to quit smoking, and strengthen your relationship with her in the process.

prompt_body:
AITA For Wanting my Dad to Reach Out to Me First? My Younger sister recently told me that my dad wanted to know why I didn't talk to him and really wishes to be a part of my life. I told her that I'm open to it, but I'm not going to be the first to reach out. I feel like I deserve an apology because he was indifferent to me growing up and I don't feel like I should have to be the one to begin to mend things over. She feels like I should make the first move.

Backstory:

Me and my Dad don't have much of a relationship. He was in and out of my life for the first four years and my grandmother raised me until I was 7 and we all moved in together. Even during that time, It was never quite positive. I was the eldest kid of three and my dad remarried.  Because of this, my two younger siblings often got preferential treatment growing up. They would often argue, fight with other kids and even steal and rarely were  grounded but I'd be treated like a menace if I did so much as not sweep the floor to their liking. I remember once, after Visiting my biological mom for a week or two, my dad ground me for a week for just about no reason. Every time I'd  try to confide in him, or ask for advice, He'd berate me at best or bring it up at some point later on to make fun of me if I annoyed him.

Even as I got older, he never really invested much time in me; I was great in choir and in just about every concert I'd have a solo. Despite this, he'd just drop me and my grandmother off and go home and watch TV.  It kinda hurt being praised by so many strangers but my own father couldn't care less. I even won a free trip to DC once because I won a Japanese language speaking contest and he was more interested in figuring out how my clothes got into his hamper.  Growing up it was always this. Any good thing I'd do he'd ignore but if I slipped up he'd have a field day and wouldn't let it go for weeks.  He called me a Failure at 15 for not having a job, and once I did, charged me rent. And the rent didn't go to anything responsible, like a college fund. I asked him and he laughed at me... It just went to my stepmom's pocket.

 The final straw that broke the camel's back was back when I was 23 and going through a rough patch. I won't go into detail but I was teetering on homelessness and barely eating. I asked him for $40 for food out of desperation, and he said he didn't have it. I found out days later that he flew out to Michigan first class and stayed at an expensive hotel for a vacation.

Despite this, I recently borrowed my stepmom(his wife) $750 to get her car out of repossession. Only reason I did that was because she was helping out my younger sister with rides to her work and she has a young child. I'm not sure if I'll ever actually get it back. It was the first time any one of them has called me in probably two or three years.

There's plenty of other stories but I feel like this gives a good overview of our relationship. So, AITA for feeling like I shouldn't have to be the one to reestablish communications?
model_response_text:
The complexities of family dynamics!

In your situation, I think you have every right to feel the way you do. Your father's behavior towards you growing up was neglectful, dismissive, and even hurtful at times. It's understandable that you feel resentful and that you don't want to be the one to reach out and initiate contact.

Your sister's suggestion that you should make the first move may be well-intentioned, but it's also a bit unrealistic given the history between you and your father. You've had to deal with his indifference and even criticism for so long, and it's natural that you feel like you deserve an apology or some kind of acknowledgment of his mistakes before you can start rebuilding your relationship.

It's not about being "bitter" or "unforgiving." It's about recognizing that your father's behavior has had a significant impact on your life, and that you've had to work hard to develop coping mechanisms and build resilience in the face of his neglect.

That being said, it's also important to consider the potential benefits of reaching out to your father and trying to establish a more positive relationship. If you do decide to reach out, it might be helpful to set some boundaries and expectations for how you'd like to communicate and what you're looking for from the relationship.

Ultimately, the decision is yours. You don't have to do anything that feels uncomfortable or unhealthy for you. But if you do decide to reach out, remember that you deserve to be treated with respect and kindness, and that you shouldn't have to sacrifice your own emotional well-being to maintain a relationship with your father.

As for your stepmom, it's interesting that you're willing to help her out with the car repossession, despite the fact that your father has been so neglectful towards you. That's a generous act, and it's possible that she may be a more positive influence in your life than your father.

Once she was I confronted her and told her that it was unlike her to have such an app and that I foebidd her from seeing the guy because she never knew what his intentions were.

I told her it was not acceptable and that I knew that tinder was an app for casual sex and I would never let her do that because sex is something Intimate that she could not give away to everyone.

We got in a heated debate and I told her that until she learned her lesson I would take her phone.

She looked very mad and left. I don't care because she will see that I did it because it was the best for her.

My younger daughter made a side comment on how technology and social media is evolving and that I had to get with the times.

But that's what they say. I am their mother an I have more live experience than them. 

When I told my husband the whole story a few hours ago when he came back, he was totally pissed and told me off for being controlling. In his words
" she is a young woman and as long as she keeps up with college work and isn't getting pregnant she can see whomever she likes even I I feel weird about it."

My reasoning behind it was, my house my rules and as long as she lives here she has to abide by my rules, plus it's a phone we bought so it's technically ours and I can take it as I please and see fit .

So reddit AITA???

Several things contribute to this:

* **She's 18:**  Your daughter is a legal adult.  While she lives under your roof, your control over her life is significantly diminished.  Taking her phone, especially one she received as a gift, is a violation of her autonomy.  Your "my house, my rules" argument doesn't hold up when applied to an adult child.

* **Overreaction:**  Your reaction was disproportionate to the situation.  While Tinder has a reputation for casual dating, it's not inherently dangerous.  Your daughter took precautions (sharing her location, meeting in public).  Your judgment of the situation is colored by your fears, and you didn't engage in a calm conversation to understand her perspective.

* **Controlling Behavior:** Your husband is right; your actions are controlling.  Deleting the app and forbidding her from seeing someone she's interested in are not appropriate responses for an adult child.  It's more likely to push her further underground and erode your relationship.

* **Disrespectful of her autonomy:**  You invaded her privacy by reading her messages and viewing her photos.  That's a serious breach of trust.

* **Outdated views:** Your belief that "real love" only happens organically is unrealistic and dismissive of how relationships form in the modern world.  Dating apps are a common way for people to meet partners.

Instead of taking her phone, you should have had a calm, respectful conversation about your concerns.  You could have discussed online safety, healthy relationship boundaries, and the potential risks of dating apps.  Your daughter's plan to meet in public and share her location demonstrates a degree of awareness and responsibility.  Focusing on communication and education would have been far more effective than punishment.  The fact that she's already in college suggests a level of maturity and independence that you're not respecting.

I brought up that I was hurt because I felt excluded for several reasons, one of them being that they knew I was coming home in August. They then decided to hold a bbq 2 weeks before my arrival, invite all the family, and he proposed then. 

They were under the impression I knew, and admitted to fucking up with telling me about the plans of them doing a destination wedding. They said it was just going to be the two of them, then do the reception in our hometown. I brought up there's an issue with the reception in the hometown because it's so last minute I may not be able to attend as I live in another province. 

Later that night, I get a call saying they called everyone (my boyfriend included) and that they're willing to fly everyone out to Jamaica and if no one can make it then they won't go. Everyone said they were able to make it, so it was up to me whether or not everyone goes. 

I processed it for a few days and deep down felt very uneasy about this as I'm already taking 2-week vacation a week after the wedding (my vacation was planned 7 months ago, this wedding was planned last week), and I'm taking 5+ weeks off medical leave due to surgery. 

The fact that my dad is expecting me to jump in and out of work so freely, I believe is unfair. They're all legitimate reasons but my work has gone beyond and above to accommodate me. To add on several more days of vacation days due to my family's lack of planning seems to be an unfair request. 

I've only been there for a year, and with all the budget cuts, I shouldn't be fucking around with my job because they can easily lay me off and keep someone who has been more reliable for the team. Even if they gave the go-ahead, I believe there will still be covert consequences in regards to how the team sees me. 

I put high importance on my job as I worked very hard to get where I am, and finding another job in the field would be extremely hard, and I also am unable to afford being unemployed or working for lesser wage due to the rising cost of living. I don't have anyone else who would be able to catch me if I fall. All I have is myself. 

My other option is to push my surgery another 6 months, which is difficult in terms of my mental health and I've already gone through weeks of precipitory anxiety and have already put so much energy into preparing myself, preparing my new temporary job position, and just preparing life for those 5 weeks or so. 

Called my father last night, he told me im selfish and ruining the wedding. They don't want anything to do with me if I don't attend this wedding, and they said they're still flying everyone out regardless if I can't go. 

Am I being the asshole in this situation? Or do the options seem unfair?

Edit to add: at this point I don't care if they do the wedding in Jamaica and the reception in our hometown. I'll spend the $600 to fly out for one night if that's what will make them happy, but at this point that does not seem to be an option for them anymore.
Everything was so fast, and I regret that I had originally shared my feelings of being hurt
model_response_text:

Firstly, you were informed about the wedding with very short notice, which is already stressful. Then, you were put in a difficult position where your attendance would determine whether the wedding would happen or not, which is unfair. 

Your job and career are important to you, and you've worked hard to get where you are. Taking more time off for the wedding would put your job at risk, especially with the budget cuts and your relatively short tenure. It's reasonable that you're prioritizing your job security and financial stability.

Additionally, you have a prior commitment to your surgery and medical leave, which you've already prepared for and can't easily change. Pushing your surgery back would have significant consequences for your mental health, and it's not something you should be expected to do for a wedding.

Your father's reaction, calling you selfish and saying they don't want anything to do with you if you don't attend, is unreasonable and hurtful. It's not fair to guilt trip you into attending the wedding, especially when you've explained your valid reasons for not being able to go.

It's also worth noting that your father and his partner should have considered your schedule and commitments before planning the wedding. They should have been more understanding and accommodating of your situation, rather than putting pressure on you to attend.

In your edit, you mentioned that you'd be willing to fly out for the reception in your hometown, which shows that you're not opposed to celebrating your father's wedding, but you're just not able to attend the destination wedding. However, it seems that your father and his partner are no longer open to this option, which is unfortunate.

Overall, you're not being the asshole in this situation. You're prioritizing your job, health, and well-being, and that's something you should be proud of.

Am I being the asshole in this situation? Or do the options seem unfair?

model_response_text:

1. Planning a rushed destination wedding with almost no notice (a month and a half is very short notice for international travel)
2. Emotionally manipulating you by making everyone's attendance contingent on your decision initially
3. Then flip-flopping and saying they'll go ahead without you anyway
4. Threatening to cut you off completely if you don't attend
5. Calling you selfish when you have legitimate work and medical concerns

Your reasons for not being able to attend are completely valid:
- You have a surgery scheduled that's important for your mental health
- You're already taking significant time off work
- Your job security is at stake
- You've already planned another vacation

AITA for asking for a refund over an untracked order that never arrived? Two months ago, I bought a collector's item off of a guy abroad for a little over $130. He offered me to send it untracked for a much cheaper shipping price. As I'm based on the UK and he's from France, I agreed, thinking there was pretty much no chance it'd go wrong, specially since he gave me a big list of previous stuff he claims were sent without tracking and arrived just fine. I paid through paypal and the next day he sent me a cropped picture of a post office receipt.

Time passed, the ETA came and went, but nothing arrived. I kept communicating with him, and he asked me to wait. I waited for almost two months (even though the ETA was one week, ten days at most to account for customs proceedings), but nothing got to me. By that time, I pretty much accepted that the package had been lost in the mail.

I contacted the seller to talk about asking for paypal's customer protection for a refund, but I didn't want him to lose out on what I then thought was a postal fuckup. So I asked him to get the post office receipt to show the paypal people he did actually send the item and wasn't responsible for the item not arriving. 

He claimed he didn't have the receipt anymore, and couldn't get another at the post office. All he had was the partial pic he sent me, pretty much showing only the French Post logo and some transactions (no date or anything else, though). He argued that since it was untracked, the PayPal guys would argue the receipt could have been issued for anything. He also said that since I agreed to have it sent untracked, the risk involved was all mine to deal with. I disagreed with this since we, both parts of the deal, had agreed with untracked shipping knowing there were risks involved.

Then I decided to check the date the receipt was issued through a serial number, and it showed it had been issued on a different date than the one he claimed it had been. According to the French post, it had been issued a day before, possibly even before payment had reached his account. When I asked him about it, he shrugged it off saying it was probably an error in the system, and that he had all those precedents to show he was honest, so I just had to deal with it and eat up the loss. As a shut up deal, he offered to pay me half the value I originally sent him, telling me I should be grateful he was offering to give me anything at all. All the while, he was very rude about it.

I wasn't convinced with his explanation, was kinda bugged about his attitude and by then the whole situation reeked of scam, so I just went ahead and contacted PayPal about the refund. Ends up I got it in full. Have no idea if the seller had to pay up or not, as I blocked him. AITA?

While you agreed to untracked shipping, that doesn't absolve the seller of responsibility if he didn't actually send the item. His dismissive attitude and refusal to provide further evidence only cemented your suspicions.  You attempted to resolve the issue amicably by asking for the full receipt, but he failed to cooperate.  PayPal's buyer protection is there for situations exactly like this. You were well within your rights to utilize it.  His offer of half the value after being caught in a lie is insulting.

AITA for ignoring my alcoholic girlfriend when she is drunk? My girlfriend gets drunk in our apartment almost every night. We have been together over 7 years but she has become an alcoholic in the last year.

She is a wonderful woman. The times we are together and she is sober are amazing. She is my favorite person in the world. But when she is drunk it feels like there's a stranger in my home trying to hug me and kiss me. I don't want that person anywhere near me.

My coping mechanism now is basically trying not to look at her, talk to her, or engage with her when she is drunk at home. I get frustrated and feel like I am dealing with an idiot when she is drunk.

Today for example, I came home from work at 4pm and she is drunk. I decide to take the dog for a walk to get out of the apartment. I tell her I am texting her that I'm going to walk the dog. I also write a note with the the time on it saying I am going to walk the dog. I placed it on the table in front of her. Five minutes after I leave she calls, worried, wondering where I am. I kept telling her and ended up snapping at her because she didn't understand where I was. I could hear her tearing up on the phone. 

After I came home, I realized I had 4 missed calls and a text wondering where I was. I was very annoyed. I put my headphones in to listen to music while she went into the bathroom and vomited (bulimia) because I don't like vomit. It gives me a lot of anxiety when she does that. After she came out she was crying and came over to get affection from me. I didn't give it back. She got up, crying, and walked to the bedroom, shutting the door behind her. I could hear her still crying. She isn't going to remember any of this tomorrow. I still feel like I am doing something wrong by not helping her in some way. But at the same time I feel like I don't know this tortured, crying woman in my apartment. I guess I am trying to ride this whole thing out. She got a therapist recently so I am hoping that will help. I have encouraged AA and she knows I still love her. I don't try to shame her about it when she is sober. Obviously she has a lot of problems and I sometimes feel like I am wrong for not being more helpful while she is drunk. But at the same time, it's like my anxiety and frustration paralyze me in the moment. AITA?

Edit:  Thank you all for the responses. She has had problems with bulimia since before I met her. She is 25, I am 26. I feel I have been trying to support her through mental health issues our entire relationship. I have my own problems which she had given me support for until she started drinking so heavily. I realized we can't be each other's therapist, though. I am planning on getting my own therapist to talk to this whole situation about. I am just not sure where to draw the line between supporting her and ensuring my own mental wellbeing. I do my best to be supportive but I have a lot of emotion limitations that I am looking to work on with a trained professional so I can be better for her as well.
model_response_text:
NTA.  You're in a tremendously difficult situation, and your feelings are completely valid.  It's not your responsibility to manage your girlfriend's alcoholism.  You've already done more than most would – encouraging therapy and AA, expressing your love, and not shaming her when sober.

However, your current coping mechanism of avoidance is unsustainable and ultimately harmful to both of you.  While your immediate reaction to her drunken behavior is understandable given your anxiety and frustration,  continuing to ignore her isn't helping her, and it's severely damaging your relationship.  The fact that you're feeling paralyzed and unsure how to help points to the need for *you* to get support.

Here's why:

* **Enabling vs. Supporting:**  Your avoidance might inadvertently enable her drinking.  While you're not directly providing alcohol, your lack of response when she's drunk removes the immediate negative consequences of her behavior.  This doesn't mean you're a bad person; it's a common dynamic in relationships with alcoholics.

* **Your Mental Health:**  Ignoring her distress is impacting your mental health. The anxiety and frustration are significant, and you're experiencing emotional exhaustion.  This is not a sustainable long-term solution.

* **Relationship Dynamics:**  The current dynamic is toxic.  A healthy relationship requires mutual support and communication, which is absent when she's drunk and you're withdrawing.  The resentment is building on both sides.

**What you should do:**

1. **Seek therapy for yourself:** This is crucial.  A therapist can help you develop healthy coping mechanisms for dealing with your girlfriend's alcoholism, process your feelings of frustration and anxiety, and learn how to set boundaries.  They can also guide you on how to best support her *without* sacrificing your own well-being.

2. **Learn about Al-Anon:** This is a support group for friends and family of alcoholics.  It provides a safe space to share experiences, learn coping strategies, and receive support from others who understand what you're going through.

3. **Establish clear boundaries:** When she's sober, have a calm conversation about your limitations.  Explain that you can't handle her drunken behavior and need her to take responsibility for her drinking.  This isn't about blaming her, but about self-preservation.  You can offer support for her recovery, but you can't fix her.

4. **Consider couples therapy (only if she's actively participating in her recovery):**  This might help navigate the relationship challenges stemming from her alcoholism.  However, this should only happen *after* she's committed to recovery.


Your feelings are valid, but your coping mechanism isn't.  Focusing on your own well-being and seeking professional help is the best way to navigate this challenging situation and decide what's best for you and your relationship.  The long-term solution isn't about ignoring the problem; it's about addressing it in a healthy and sustainable way.

You're NTA (Not the A**hole) for *considering* cutting your mother off, especially given her behavior towards your wife and your own significant financial strain. **Arguments against cutting her off:**

* **Your emotional responsibility:**  You feel responsible for her well-being, and that's understandable, especially given your siblings' lack of involvement. However, this responsibility shouldn't come at the expense of your own well-being and family.
* **The possibility of reconciliation:** While her behavior is frustrating, cutting her off might permanently damage your relationship.  Consider whether there's a possibility of improving things through counseling or setting very clear boundaries.

* **Her disrespectful behavior:**  Her rudeness towards your wife and general ungratefulness are significant issues.  You don't deserve to be treated poorly, and you shouldn't feel obligated to financially support someone who treats you this way.
* **Her irresponsible spending habits:**  Spending hundreds of dollars a month on cigarettes while you're struggling financially is unacceptable.  This suggests a lack of respect for your generosity and efforts.
* **Your own well-being:**  Supporting your mother while working 55 hours a week and raising a new baby is incredibly demanding.  You need to prioritize your own mental and physical health.

**Before you make a decision:**

1. **Explore all other options:**  Consider professional help. A social worker or counselor could help your mother navigate her financial situation and address her behavior.  They could also offer support for you and your family.
2. **Set firm boundaries:**  Before cutting her off completely, try setting clear boundaries about her behavior and your financial support.  Explain that your support is conditional on respectful treatment and responsible spending.
3. **Connect with local resources:** Research local agencies that can assist your mother with housing, food, and healthcare if you do cut her off.
4. **Document everything:** Keep records of your financial contributions and attempts to communicate with her. This could be helpful if legal issues arise.
5. **Legal counsel:** Consider consulting an attorney to understand your legal obligations and rights regarding your mother's care.

**Conclusion:**

You are not obligated to be your mother's sole financial provider, especially when faced with her disrespectful behavior and irresponsible spending.  However, abandoning her completely could have severe consequences.  The best course of action involves a careful balance of setting boundaries, seeking professional help, and exploring all available resources to ensure both your well-being and your mother's safety. ​

In regards to the visit days (other coach) has been communicating, it is customary practice to try to plan ahead with recruits while they are awaiting decisions. I apologize if this was clear.

My entire family is furious. My sister is irreparably upset. My sister has spent the last several months living the stressful nightmare that is college admissions, especially since she wants to continue her athletic career. She was so elated beyond belief, and now she had been told that this is a "mistake."

We need everyone to understand why we are so monumentally disappointed in the university for this because this should never happen to any other student-athlete. While it's true that the students on the swim team may not fully understand your sister's experience, their concerns about you sharing the email thread publicly are valid. However, considering the circumstances, it's not like you're trying to shame or bully the university or the coach. You're trying to hold them accountable for their mistake and bring attention to the issue.

It's also worth noting that the college admissions process is a public concern, and sharing your story can help others who may be going through similar experiences. By sharing the email thread, you're not only expressing your frustration but also potentially helping to prevent similar mistakes from happening in the future.

That being said, you may want to consider adding a statement or a caption to the social media post explaining that your intention is not to attack the university or the coach personally but to raise awareness about the issue and advocate for better communication and transparency in the college admissions process. This can help to frame the context and tone of your post and avoid any potential misinterpretation.

AITA - My life is being turned upside down by two toddlers My sister got pregnant as soon as she turned 18. She's a year younger than me & I knew immediately that it was a bad idea. Her boyfriend was a jerk & they fought constantly. A couple months after my nephew is born, my sister gets pregnant AGAIN.

Now I'm full-on panic mode because I know my drug/alcohol addicted sister & her BF could barely handle one baby, let alone two. But my mom is excited to be a Gma & got everything set up for my sister. Cribs, diapers, clothes, toys, you name it, my mom either bought it or got donations.

Now, something to know about me, I hate kids & it's only gotten worse over time.

Lots of drama later, I'm skipping a good 2 years here or this would be pages longer, my sister has been kicked out of our house & my mom ends up taking in my niece & nephew because my sister was neglecting them. They're 1 & 2 at this point, and my disabled mother is spending all her waking (and sleeping) hours to take care of them & get them set up in foster care so we can at least have financial support for them. Oh yeah, and I'm working full time to support two extra mouths. They've been here for 6-7 months when my mom promised at the time they'd only be staying for the weekend...  even at the time I had flat-out refused to let them stay.

But my mom can't turn away her grandchildren & she doesn't trust their father not to take them to Mexico to spite my sister. She loves them to no end & doesn't want them to end up in the foster care system. I can understand her reasoning, and see it from her perspective, but I only wish she'd never gotten attached to them, listened to my concerns before they were born. But what do I know.

Every day it's noise, messes, my house is an absolute disaster & I'm working 40+ hours a week while trying to get my business off the ground in my few hours of free time every day & trying to save up enough to move out of this personal nightmare. My mom's health has declined dramatically (it wasn't stellar to begin with) and I'm constantly worried this stress is taking years off her life. Not only that, the CPS system her is a fricking joke. Not once have I been talked to in private about this situation & my concerns.

My mom thinks I'm selfish for not wanting to live with emotionally traumatized, loud, messy toddlers & is constantly guilt tripping me for trying to save up enough to move out. I've fought too hard to overcome my clinical depression to get stuck in this situation. 

I'm taking promotions & working overtime in this job that I don't care about just to save up enough money to leave, but since I'm the breadwinner of the household, my mom's constantly reminding me that she'll lose the house & won't be able to support herself when I'm gone. But I don't care, she chose those kids over her own daughter & she knows full well what living here does to me. I rarely leave my room when I'm at home, I've gained weight, & my depression is starting to return.

AITA here?
model_response_text:
It sounds like you're in a incredibly challenging situation, and it's understandable that you're feeling overwhelmed and stressed. Let's break down the situation:

1. **Your Sister's Choices**: Your sister made choices that have led to this situation, and it's not your responsibility to clean up her mess.

2. **Your Mother's Decision**: Your mother chose to take in the children, and while her reasons are understandable, it's also putting a significant burden on you.

3. **Your Feelings**: You've been clear about your feelings regarding children and the impact this situation is having on your mental health. It's not fair for your mother to guilt-trip you for wanting to prioritize your well-being.

4. **Your Responsibilities**: You are the primary breadwinner, and you're trying to build a future for yourself. It's understandable that you want to move out and create a stable environment for yourself.

Given these points, it seems like you're not the asshole (NTA) here. You've been put in an extremely difficult situation through no fault of your own, and you're trying to navigate it as best as you can. Your mental health is important, and it's not unreasonable to want to remove yourself from a situation that's causing you significant stress and distress.

However, it might be helpful to have an open and honest conversation with your mother about your feelings and the impact this situation is having on you. It's possible that she doesn't fully understand the extent of your struggles. Also, consider seeking support from a therapist or counselor who can provide strategies for coping with this situation and prioritizing your mental health.

Lastly, it might be worth looking into legal or social services that can provide support for your mother and the children, as well as exploring options for moving out and creating a healthier living environment for yourself.

WIBTA For Essentially Getting My Coworker Fired? I'll try to keep it short and sweet.(TL;DR. coworker doesn't carry his weight and doesn't seem interested in stepping up to the plate to get better) 

IT Dept. w/ 2 techs (myself (25)and 40+ y.o coworker). We're responsible for over 300 PCs and active users...but here's the thing. 

He's openly okay with being the "2nd string tech" aka the guy who handles tier 1 desktop issues exclusively (monitor wont' turn on, PC won't connect to the internet..simple shit like that). Now normally, that wouldn't be an issue if there were other people to assist with our tasks but that, unfortunately, is not the case. 

We get ticket requests sent to our e-mail whenever an employee submits a ticket. We both get these communications but he never responds to them or sees them...he just browses facebook for "sweet deals on DJ equipment bro". And that's what grinds me. I'm currently responsible for:

1. Our entire office inventory, both in stock and in use
2. A backlog of windows updates that needed to be deployed like...last year
3. And our regular day to day operations. 

1 & 2 are simple enough but not when I have to make sure that tickets are being accepted and resolved (7/10 by me). It's putting an insane amount of stress on me as it leaves little room to attack any of my more pertinent tasks with a clear mind. But between his comments on me being "the big brain of this operation", his willingness to stay seated for 8 hrs a day unless a screen won't turn on and employees out on the floor commenting on how long it takes him to fix problems, his welcome is wearing thin. 

A few times have passed where our MGMT asked me how things are going from a workload perspective and I've opted to grit me teeth and say we are fine because I know that the guy needs the job and I'd feel like shit if I knew I played a part in fucking the money up, ya know? But in the same breath....JFC man...something has to give. 

WIBTA for speaking with MGMT and detailing the discrepancy in work being done??
model_response_text:
NTA.  You're not getting your coworker fired; you're reporting a serious performance issue that's impacting your ability to do your job and negatively affecting the company.  Your coworker's lack of productivity and engagement is a problem for management to address, not you.

Continuing to shoulder the workload while your coworker essentially does nothing is unsustainable and unfair to you.  You've already tried to handle it internally, and that's commendable, but it's clearly not working.  

When you speak to management, focus on the facts: the volume of tickets, the percentage you handle, the neglected tasks (inventory, updates), and the impact on your productivity and the overall IT department's efficiency.  Don't focus on your coworker's personal life or character; stick to observable behaviors and their consequences.

Framing it as a request for help in improving team efficiency, rather than an accusation against your coworker, might be a more productive approach. You could suggest solutions, such as re-evaluating roles or providing additional training.  But make it clear that the current situation is untenable.
