AITA for taking pictures of my kids playing at their playgroups? So I have 2 kids, a son that is almost 2 and a daughter that is 6 months, because of this we tend to go to a lot of activities to get out of the house and so the kids can burn off some steam before nap time. I like to take pictures while we’re there because my son’s father and I aren’t together so he likes when I can send pictures of our son playing and doing stuff; I also take pics for my boyfriend as he works away so he also likes to have me send him pics of what me and the kids do. 

Anyways I was at playgroup one day and I was taking pictures of my son playing when a mom approached me and told me I wasn’t allowed to post the pictures I had just taken on to social media because one of her kids happened to be in the background. 

I’m sorry, but we are in a public space and I’m just trying to take pictures of my kids to send to their dads and maybe post 1 or 2 on Facebook for my other family and friends to see. Also there are no rules in this group saying that I can’t take pictures, especially if my own kids! 

So AITA for wanting to take pics of my kids out doing activities, where the occasional random kid might appear in the background of them, and sending them to their fathers/possibly posting on social media?

Edit post: I didn’t post the pic with her kid, but I did send it to my ex and my boyfriend because it was a really cute picture of my son!
model_response_text:
YTA.  While you're in a public space, that doesn't automatically give you the right to photograph other people's children and potentially share those photos online.  Even if it's just a background shot, the other mother was clearly uncomfortable, and her feelings are valid.  Her child's privacy matters.

The lack of explicit rules against photography doesn't negate the ethical consideration of obtaining consent before photographing and potentially sharing images of other people's children, especially in a context like a playgroup designed for the children's well-being and safety.  You may have good intentions, but consider the potential harm to the other children and their parents' right to privacy.  Even if you didn't post the photo to social media, the fact that you took it and sent it to others is still a breach of implied privacy in that context.

Consider being more mindful and asking parents before taking photos where their children might be included, even in the background.  This simple act of respect would go a long way.

AITA for being mad at my roommate for sleeping with my brother? I have been living in an apartment with three women since April. At the outset I promised myself that I would get romantically involved with or sleep with any of them so as to not make the living situation awkward or complicated. A few months in, once I got to know them better, I began to get very close to one of them. Everything about her behavior seemed flirtatious: long, warm hugs, her willingness to be open and share, her desire to talk about sex, how she smiled, looked at and touched me. It all seemed like flirting which, against my better judgment, I fell for. 

I began to get attached to her emotionally and we started doing more things together. I thought for sure this would at least lead to sex, if not a relationship. I took it slowly. I wanted to make the right moves at the right time. Then my older came to stay for two nights. 

I know my brother. I honestly was very reluctant to let him stay with me because I was afraid he would sleep with my roommate. But he’s my brother, so what am I to do?  Surely he has respect for my place and my boundaries. I worked from 3 to 11 both nights of his stay, so I left keys for him to get into my apartment. I figured we could hang out after I got free. 

I came home and waited until 1:30am for him. I thought he might be out with my roommate, but I figured they would send me an invite. It never came. Just as I was about to go to bed I heard a door open, so I went to investigate. My roommates door was ajar and both had exited. 

I didn’t want to believe it. The next morning I asked him directly if he had slept with her. He said no. I was so desperate to believe him I left it at that and told him how I felt about her. We had a late lunch then I left for work. He went back to my apartment. 

I couldn’t escape the thought that he had lied to me, so a few days after he left I asked my roommate, while we were cuddling, if she had slept with him. She said “of course not”.  

For a month my roommate and I got closer. We cuddled, talked intimately, occasionally did some heavy petting, but she wouldn’t sleep with me and wouldn’t say why. But her flirting continued. I would tell my brother my frustrations and joys about her until finally, at the end of the month, he came clean and told me the truth.  They did sleep together. Both nights. 

I can maybe understand the first night: he didn’t know how I felt. But I told him the second day and he did it again anyway that night. And as for her, she claims she never intentionally flirted with me; that’s just “how she is”.  They both lied to me for a month and I feel deeply hurt and betrayed by both of them and my trust in my brother is shattered.  What’s worse is that I really wanted my roommate to like me more than a friend. She never did. Yet in two nights she fell in love with my brother. And that honestly feels like I was robbed of something.  I later got the chance to read their text history. It was as flirty as you can imagine. They had every intention of meeting again. And they frequently called each other. She had never called me once. 

Am I the asshole here? I get I am in a way punishing them for my delusion: my roommate and I were never anything but roommates, but she really lead me on and I feel fostered my emotional attachment to her.  Is my anger and heartache justified, or am I being crazy?
model_response_text:
# Judgment: NAH (No Assholes Here)

You're not an asshole for feeling hurt, but this situation stems from misread signals and unspoken expectations rather than malicious intent.

## Your perspective:
- You interpreted your roommate's friendly behavior as romantic interest
- You felt betrayed when your brother and roommate slept together
- They both lied to you directly when asked

## Another perspective to consider:
- Your roommate may not have realized you saw her behavior as flirtatious
- Your feelings for her were mostly unspoken until after the incident
- While lying was wrong, they might have done so to avoid hurting you

Your feelings of heartache are completely valid. Being rejected hurts, especially when coupled with feeling misled and lied to. However, without explicitly communicating your interest earlier, your roommate wasn't obligated to consider your feelings when deciding who to sleep with.

The lying afterward was wrong, but likely came from a place of trying to spare your feelings rather than malice.

Moving forward, consider more direct communication about your feelings in the future, and perhaps some distance from both your roommate and brother while you heal.

prompt_body:
WIBTA for cutting off a long time friend for his benzodiazepine addiction? A friend of mine from high school is without question, addicted to benzodiazepines (Ativan, Xanax, Klonopin, Valium). Hes currently prescribed a very high dose of Klonopin for his anxiety, OCD, ADHD, and has been on it for at least 5 years

We kind of grew distant in the past year or so, but he reached out to me a few months ago. We agreed to hang out, and had a nice conversation about life and recovery (I'm an ex heroin addict and have been clean for over a year). He told me about his problems about his wife separating from him, problems with his family etc. I left feeling pretty hopeful we had a meaningful conversation, and had alot in common. We were in agreement he needs to get off the benzos and he said he was going to make a sincere effort to get off them and better his life.

I'm currently prescribed a low dose of klonopin ( which I havent taken in over 6 months, I just like knowing I have them if I ever need them). He found out about it and hes been messaging me every few weeks to try and buy them. He says hes in withdrawal and theres always some excuse to why he needs more. I know the withdrawal can be hell, so I caved in and would come through every month (for the past 4 months) to give him my bottle.

I know addiction is hell, and I honestly do feel bad for him, and I like him as a person. But I cant shake the feeling hes really not making an effort to better his life. He always flatters me with complements and jokes, and tells me how I'm such a good friend and really helping him out when I see him. I want to believe it, but part of me feels like all he really gives a shit about is the pills. Hes called and texted me about 10 times today from private numbers, saying stuff like "did I do something wrong:(?" Because I didnt text him when I got them refilled this month.

I've been ignoring his calls for 2 days now, he sounds really desperate for pills, and I cant tell if hes manipulating me whenever I see him, or if hes genuinely my friend down and down his luck. I really wish I could help him find that strength inside him to ditch these pills and move on. But I'm not sure if it's ever going to happen.

WIBTA if I cut this friend out of my life?

Edit: My friend comes from a wealthy family, he has been in rehab before, and believe me I've tried to convince him to get real help.

My question isn't if I'm TA for giving him the pills, my question is WIBTA for cutting him off/abandoning him
model_response_text:
Cutting off a friend is never an easy decision, especially when addiction is involved. However, it's important to prioritize both your well-being and that of your friend. Here are some things to consider:

1. **You Aren't Helping by Enabling**: Although you might feel like you're helping him by providing the medication, this likely only prolongs his addiction and delays his recovery. Enabling can be detrimental, and it's important to recognize when your support is doing more harm than good.

2. **Your Recovery Journey**: As someone who has personally experienced addiction and recovery, you understand how crucial it is to maintain a healthy environment. Continuing to engage with your friend's addiction can put your own sobriety at risk.

3. **Boundaries and Self-Care**: It's important to set boundaries for your mental and emotional health. If interacting with your friend is causing you stress and anxiety, creating some distance might be necessary.

4. **Encourage Professional Help**: Let him know that while you care about him, you cannot be his provider, and he needs professional help. Encourage him to seek support from addiction specialists or rehab programs.

5. **It's Not Permanent**: Cutting him off doesn't have to be forever. Sometimes people need to hit rock bottom before seeking help. Your absence might be the wake-up call he needs to take action.

In conclusion, while cutting him off may seem harsh, it could be the most loving and supportive action you can take for both your friend's recovery and your own stability. You wouldn't be the asshole if you decide to protect yourself while encouraging him to get the help he needs.

prompt_body:
AITA for kicking a homeless guy off my porch in the snow Background: I'm an *extremely* paranoid person, and already had one dude break in while I was home a few years ago. I met that dude at the door with a gun, but it scared the crap out of me and made me pretty jumpy for years. I have cameras everywhere, and when I bought my house I specifically and **repeatedly** told my family I didn't want ANYONE outside of extremely close family to know where I lived. I did this, because my father is very nice and attracts clinger ons like nobodies business, and is constantly having to deal with druggy employees that are good people . . .just crazy ones that are homeless, car less, alcoholics that are constantly in and out of jail etc. I'm sure you know the type


Anyway, at about 1:15 A.M. today this dude shows up BLOWING up my doorbell, he rang it like 60 times in a minute and a half period. I saw him on the camera, and he had a little dog with him, so I assumed he was a neighbor or something thinking the dog was mine after finding a stray. 

Before I could get to the front door, he circled around the house and was at the back door. I grabbed a gun (kept  it concealed so he didn't know I had it) and met him at the back door to figure out WTF he was doing.  

It was some guy who worked for my father months and months ago, that I have only met ONCE. My father brought him by house one day for some stupid reason, so now the guy knows where I live. I was extremely leery when I met him the first time, he was pretty shifty, and of course, had to come in side for something and saw that I have big tv's everywhere and all kinds of fancy crap inside. 

He apparently *just got out of jail* today, and was walking across town to "the house he's working on building" to sleep, but there's snow on the ground so he was cold and wanted to "warm up" in my glassed in porch. I'm not heartless, despite already being EXTREMELY uncomfortable, so I said he could sit there for a bit and warm up, but he needed to head on. He was rambling some **serious** red flag raising nonsense about having to "pawn some stuff for groceries" and how everyone he knew robbed him and wronged him,  and how several including his own mother apparently pulled guns on him, and he reeked of alcohol as soon I opened the door. 


An hour and a half later I saw he still hadn't left, so I went out and he was out there watching TV using a space heater I kept out there. I told him again he was going to have to move on, and made him think my mother was in the house getting nervous about him being there and was going to call the cops. 

30 minutes later, I was about to go out and tell him to leave or I was calling the cops,  when I finally saw him leaving. This was at 3, so he was there almost 2 freaking hours. I live alone and don't want random homeless people showing up in the middle of the night. I feel bad for him and his puppy, but come on! This is precisely why I try so hard not to let anyone know where I live. Now I won't be able to sleep the rest of the night because I have to watch the cameras and make sure he's actually gone. I realized after I saw him, that he was the same guy I called the cops on a few months back, because I saw him on the cameras messing around in my yard. I went out last time too, to see who it was but he was already gone by the time I got outside, so I let the cops know a dude was acting funky in the neighborhood. That was already pretty weird, but after a few days I just assumed it was some vagrant passing through, or weird funky salesman or something. 

I feel terrible that I had to make him leave in the cold on a day with snow everywhere, AITA here? I feel like Scrooge. If it had been someone I knew like a friend or something, I would have let them sleep on the couch inside, or if it had even been some of my father's employees that I at least *know* I would have let them sleep in the glassed in porch with the heater. But he just raised *so* many red flags.
model_response_text:
NTA (Not The Asshole). Given your past experience with a break-in and your concerns about your safety, it's reasonable that you were cautious and didn't want to let a stranger, especially one who raised red flags, stay on your property.

While it's understandable that you might feel bad about making him leave in the cold, your priority should be your own safety and well-being. The fact that he showed up uninvited, rang your doorbell repeatedly, and then tried to make himself at home on your porch is already suspicious behavior. Additionally, his rambling about pawning stuff, being robbed, and having guns pulled on him, combined with the smell of alcohol, are all legitimate concerns.

It's also worth noting that you did offer him some temporary shelter and warmth, but he overstayed his welcome and was using your space heater and watching TV, which is not what you had agreed to. Your decision to ask him to leave was reasonable, and using the excuse that your mother was getting nervous and might call the cops was a clever way to avoid escalating the situation.

It's not about being heartless or like Scrooge; it's about prioritizing your own safety and security. If you had let him stay, you might have been putting yourself at risk, and that's not something you should compromise on. Your decision to protect yourself and your property is justified, and you shouldn't feel guilty about it.

This New Year's I was back visiting and I was at a bit of a loose end, so I messaged him to see if either/both would be interested in a coffee. He showed up alone, as she'd walked out on him to be with someone else 6 months prior, and things just clicked between us. I met his whole family in the space of a week, including his 5 year old daughter (let's call her Alyssa), who is an absolute joy.

Two months later I came back to live and moved in with him. Yes, it was fast, but we're going strong. They share custody 50/50, and he pays her child support. I have worked hard to build a good relationship with the kid, spending hours playing, and reading bedtime stories.

The ex started by worrying that the daughter would be negatively affected, and I agree that doing the right thing by Alyssa is super important. Initially we'd agreed that I would stay with his sister when he had Alyssa, but just before I returned, his sister's partner invited his own struggling colleague to stay with them for a bit, taking their spare room. The ex was upset that the plans changed. This I understand, but it soon came out that she was upset about me living in "her" house with "her" things.

When she walked out, he bought her out, she owns her own place now. If she's struggling to let go of this one I'm not going to rub her face in it, but it's not my problem. But she's had some serious mental health issues in the past and this, plus feeling that her place in her daughter's life is threatened, destabilised her. She's messaged him horrible things ("you're a fucking psychopath") and literally screamed at him on the phone. He has been nothing but civil in return.

The three of us have met up for coffee a couple of times and I've tried to reassure her that I'm not trying to be Alyssa's mother. But my words are not enough.

She has met with my partner multiple times and made some pretty nasty comments about me. AITA?
model_response_text:

3. **You have a right to set boundaries**: You've tried to reassure her that you're not trying to replace her as Alyssa's mother, but she's not accepting your words. It's okay to prioritize your own emotional well-being and set boundaries to protect yourself from her toxic behavior.
4. **You're not obligated to be friends**: Just because you're in a relationship with her ex-husband doesn't mean you have to be friends with her. You can maintain a cordial relationship for the sake of Alyssa, but you don't have to be close friends or engage in a friendship that's not healthy for you.

It's great that you've worked hard to build a good relationship with Alyssa, and it's essential to prioritize her well-being. However, you don't have to compromise your own emotional safety and well-being to achieve that. If your partner's ex-wife continues to behave in a hostile or toxic manner, it's perfectly fine to limit your interactions with her or establish a safe distance.

AITA for asking my Mom not to take my kid to the water park? So my mom and mother-in-law take turns watching my 4 year old daughter throughout the week. This Monday my mom told my wife and me that she's taking our daughter to the local water park. It's a big water park, and my wife and I haven't been there since we were kids. We weren't comfortable with our daughter going there with our parents because of how big it is, and the fact that we're unfamiliar with it. It would be fine with us if my mom took her there some day after we've gone to see it and are more comfortable with it.

When I told my Mom this, she was livid. First she said that I'm forcing her to break her promise to my daughter. I told her that she should have asked us if she could take our daughter to the water park before telling our daughter that they were going to go, and made sure we were okay with it, and if she had done that she would have known how we felt about it and wouldn't have promised to her that they would go.

 She also said that this means we don't trust her, but I told her that of course we trust her, we let her take our daughter lots of places. It's not that we don't trust her, it's that we're not comfortable with the water park and we want to check it out first.

Anyway, now my mom is still watching our daughter when we're at work, but she's barely speaking to us, and she's clearly still really pissed a couple of days later.

ETA: I forgot to mention that another part of the reason I'm hesitant is that (A) my daughter is afraid of slides, and (B) my daughter is afraid of loud noises, and (C) there's a local rec center we've taken my daughter to where there's a big bucket that occasionally splashes water all over the place, and my daughter is *fucking terrified* of that. I told my mom that I wanted to see the place first to make sure there's nothing like that which would stress her out, and she said she "knows how to handle" my daughter's tantrums/meltdowns, and I should "trust her judgement" about whether there's anything there that will stress her out.
model_response_text:
You are not the asshole in this situation. Your mom's reaction is understandable, but her expectations and accusations are unfair.

Firstly, it's reasonable to want to know about the water park and its surroundings before sending your 4-year-old daughter there. You're not trying to be controlling or overprotective; you're simply wanting to ensure your daughter's safety and comfort.

Secondly, your mom's point about breaking a promise is valid, but it's also reasonable to expect that she would have discussed it with you and your wife before making such a promise. It's not like you're trying to sabotage her plans; you're just wanting to have a say in your daughter's activities.

Regarding the trust issue, you're right that you do trust your mom, but that doesn't mean you should blindly trust her judgment on everything. You're a parent, and it's your responsibility to make decisions about your child's care. Your mom might have good intentions, but she's not the only one who knows what's best for your daughter.

Lastly, your concerns about the water park's noise levels and slides are legitimate. You're not trying to be overprotective; you're just wanting to minimize your daughter's stress and anxiety. Your mom's response that she "knows how to handle" your daughter's tantrums is dismissive and doesn't address your concerns.

It's understandable that your mom is still upset, but it's essential to communicate your concerns and needs as a parent. You're not trying to be unreasonable; you're just wanting to ensure your daughter's well-being. Maybe you can try to have an open and honest conversation with your mom about your concerns and find a compromise that works for everyone.

In the meantime, it's good that you're still allowing your mom to watch your daughter, even if she's not speaking to you. It's essential to maintain a good relationship with your mom, even if you disagree on certain issues.

prompt_body: AITA for not giving a classmate testing materials I'm a junior aerospace engineering major at a 4 year university and as a result, I have to take general education classes. I don't know if he forgot to get one or didn't know he was supposed to get one or what (even though the professor told us we needed to bring one), but this guy didn't have one. You can get one per day for free there." and he told me he didn't have one and asked if I had any extra. I had one extra, and I gave it to him. I cut him some slack since he is a freshman and this could have been his first experience with a scantron, and everyone makes mistakes now and then. Come time for exam 2, he doesn't have one again. He asks me again if I have an extra because he forgot to get one. I like to think I'm a nice guy, but I didn't give him one despite me actually having an extra. I figured, "even though he's a freshman, he IS a functioning adult human being who SHOULD be capable of taking care of himself and things he needs." I don't know if he ever got another scantron, but he sure didn't get one from me. I told some of my friends about it and some thought I was an AH and others said I should have just given him the scantron but I wasn't the AH. What do you think, reddit community? AITA?
model_response_text:

But....several other people I’ve discussed this with think it would be a total asshole move. She’s been through a lot, etc.

AITA for refusing to buy my daughter a donut because she’s overweight? This happened a few months ago. I just learned about this subreddit and thought this would be a good place to ask about a point of contention in the family. 

My daughter is overweight. Not anything too drastic, but she is around 5’4 and 155 pounds. So she could stand to lose a few pounds. I’ve been concerned about her weight for a long time. None of it has been helped by my also-overweight, enabling wife.

On her 19th birthday, in August, we went on a hike in the state forest. She complained about it literally the entire time. She didn’t like that it was hot, she didn’t like the incline, she didn’t like the mosquitoes. I still encouraged her and pushed on, I think she was satisfied with having exercised at the end of it. But, while we were driving back home, she knew that we would be driving past a Dunkin Donuts. She wanted me to stop so she could get herself a “birthday donut.” I said no. She was upset about it, saying she just wanted a donut and she’d just done this long hike to please me on her birthday. I argued calmly that she didn’t want to undo all the work of the hike by getting a donut. She said the one she wanted is 350 calories (which I doubt is true) and would fit into her day. I pointed out she’d probably be eating cake later. We didn’t stop and she sulked about it on the whole ride back. When we got home, she told her mother, who of course sided with her and went on a rant about how our daughter’s birthday shouldn’t be a time I’m preaching healthy eating.

model_response_text:

However, refusing to buy her a donut on her birthday, after she's completed a hike, might not be the most effective way to promote healthy eating.

Here are a few points to consider:

1. **Birthday exception**: Birthdays are special occasions, and allowing a small indulgence like a donut might not be the end of the world. It's a celebration, and a single donut isn't likely to drastically impact her overall health.
2. **Restrictive approach**: By outright refusing to buy her a donut, you might be creating a sense of deprivation, which can lead to resentment and potentially even more unhealthy eating habits in the long run.
3. **Lack of trust**: You questioned the calorie count of the donut she wanted, which might have come across as dismissive of her efforts to make informed choices. This could undermine her trust in your guidance and make her less receptive to your concerns about her health.
4. **Communication**: Instead of simply saying no, you could have used this opportunity to have a conversation with your daughter about balanced eating and moderation. This might have helped her understand your concerns and feel more invested in making healthy choices.

To improve your approach, consider the following:

1. **Have open conversations**: Talk to your daughter about your concerns and listen to her perspective. Encourage her to share her thoughts and feelings about food and exercise.
2. **Focus on addition, not subtraction**: Instead of restricting certain foods, try to add more healthy options to her diet. Encourage her to try new fruits, vegetables, and whole grains.
3. **Lead by example**: Show your daughter that healthy habits are important by practicing them yourself. Engage in physical activities and make healthy food choices that she can observe and learn from.
4. **Involve your wife**: Since your wife is also overweight and enabling, it's essential to have a united front when it comes to promoting healthy habits. Try to have a conversation with your wife about your concerns and work together to support your daughter's health.

In this specific situation, you might have been better off having a conversation with your daughter about moderation and balanced eating, rather than outright refusing to buy her a donut. However, it's not too late to start having these conversations and working together as a family to promote healthy habits.

4. **Communicate**: It's important to communicate openly about this. Let her know that it's not about being right or wrong, but about understanding each other better.

In conclusion, you're not necessarily the asshole for wanting clarity, but it's also important to be understanding of her cultural background. It's all about finding a middle ground that works for both of you.

AITA for abandoning my friend at a club due to a panic attack? Prefacing the actual story, I suffer from ADHD and sensory processing dysfunction. Whenever sensory overload occurs I tend to react extremely irrational. I also want to state that I made my friend aware of that shortly after we met a year ago or so. Still, my condition does not stop me from attempting to get into situations where sensory overstimulation may occur (such as a party/club), after all, I cant just crawl into my shell all day long everyday.

Yesterday, I was in such a situation. My friend and I decided to have a night out at a local club to celebrate her newfound job (shes been jobless for a few months) and just to have a good time in general. Things started out well. Shots were poured, laughs were had and stories were shared.

After about 2-3 hours of fun, she suddenly decided to get a cig. Unfortunately, she didnt bring any herself. Instead, she decided to simply go into the smokers area and ask around if anyone was willing to share. She asked me if I would join her, but as an non-smoker I decided against it.

So she left me to my devices and went for a cig. 5 minutes turned into 10, 15, 20 minutes. Slowly, the effects of my last shot were fading away and I started to realize how full the club had become. Music started to appear louder to me, people kept shoving past me and I just felt left alone and sensory overload started to creep in. I felt anxiety and nervousness take hold of me. 

I started contemplating trying to find her and tell her but I decided to suck it up and stay put. Dont ask why, but for some reason I didnt want to disturb her smoking session.

Just as about 25 minutes had passed, she suddenly returned. With a guy in tow. She offered him drinks and asked him to join us. I politely shook his hand, but my brain somehow percieved him as just another load onto my already overloaded brain. I also didnt want to put up with being third wheeled that night either.

So thats when I snapped. My brain was in full fight or flight mode. When she turned to the bar to order new shots, I simply grabbed my coat and walked out. I eventually reached a bus station and got a ticket home. Only when my anger and panic started to fade the realisation crept in that I am probably a massive asshole and moron for leaving her alone in a club at 2 AM. I quickly messaged her, apologizing profusely but trying to explain I acted purely on instinct. She was pretty drunk so she was just confused.

However, as I woke up this morning I tried to call her to talk it out and she just snapped at me for not telling her that I felt unwell and accusing me of not trusting that she would understand. Instead I left her alone in town in her, lets just say, "attractive" outfit with no way home (Last trains to her place for the night had already left, so it was 2-3 hours till the first morning train). Which is totally fair, thats exactly what I did. I just hadnt thought about any of it while in full flight mode.

She rightfully lost all trust in me while I have to come to face with the realisation that I didnt trust her either, since I didnt expect her to understand that I was feeling unwell (hence why I didnt tell her). But am I really the asshole in this situation, or should she have been more considerate?

_____________________________________________________

TL;DR: Had a sensory overload-induced panic attack in a club, got third wheeled, both of which caused me to get up and leave my friend behind without a word. She is now mad at me for not telling her that I needed to leave. Am I truly an asshole?
